back: $F \leq \mu R$, with $F = \mu R$ in limiting equilibrium and when sliding.
At rest but on the point of moving: friction has its maximum value μR.
μ, a dimensionless number depending on the two surfaces; μ = 0 for a smooth surface.

front: Particle about to slip on a slope with no other forces

back: Opposite to the motion that would take place without friction (or to the actual motion if sliding).

front: Pulling at an angle above the horizontal
back: $R = mg - P\sin\theta$: the pull reduces the reaction and so the maximum friction.
Find the friction needed for equilibrium by resolving; if it exceeds μR the particle moves.

front: Force P up a rough slope
back: About to slide down: $P = mg\sin\alpha - \mu R$. About to move up: $P = mg\sin\alpha + \mu R$.
notes: Here P acts parallel to the slope, so R = mg cos α.
